title: Which share of a roti is greater, one fifth or one ninth?
description: One roti is shared equally among five children and another of the same size among nine. Laying one share on the other shows which fraction is greater, and the equal parts get their name, fractional units. Keeko's doubt, that one ninth is greater because nine is bigger than five, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same whole shared among more people gives a smaller fractional unit. Watch for students who think one ninth is greater because nine is bigger than five.

video_script.why: The child compares two unit fractions by thinking of them as shares of the same roti, and meets the name fractional unit.
video_script.substitution: Read one fifth as one child's share when five children share one roti, and one ninth as a share among nine.
video_script.anchor: One roti shared equally among five children, and one roti of the same size shared equally among nine
video_script.wrong_answer: one ninth is greater because nine is bigger than five
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one ninth is greater because nine is bigger than five. A ninth piece laid on a fifth piece covers only part of it, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: One fifth is greater than one ninth

final_answer.spoken: one fifth is greater than one ninth

never_show: Keeko's claim written as an inequality
maths_rules: 1 roti cut into 5 equal pieces: each piece is 1/5 roti
1 roti of the same size cut into 9 equal pieces: each piece is 1/9 roti
more sharers of the same whole means a smaller share, so 1/9 < 1/5 and 1/5 > 1/9
a fractional unit is one of the equal parts of one whole, such as 1/5 or 1/9
slip: 9 > 5 does not make 1/9 bigger; more sharers means smaller pieces
video_script.design: One idea: more sharers, smaller fractional unit. Assumes halves and fourths of a roti. Wrong idea: a bigger bottom number means a bigger share. The two rotis stay on the board to the end.
